Paper Content:
The Energy Barrier of Precritical Nuclei in Hard Spheres is Consistent with
Predictions
Lars K¨urten,1 Antoine Castagn`ede,2 Frank Smallenburg,2 and C. Patrick Royall1
1Gulliver UMR 7083, CNRS, ESPCI Paris, Universit´e PSL, 75005 Paris, France
2Laboratoire de Physique des Solides, CNRS, Universit´e Paris-Saclay, 91405 Orsay, France
Predicting crystal nucleation is among the most significant long–standing challenges in condensed
matter. In the system most studied (hard sphere colloids), the comparison between experiments
performed using static light scattering and computer simulations is woeful, with a discrepancy of over
10 orders of magnitude. The situation with other well-studied materials (such as water and sodium
chloride) is no better. It has thus far proven impossible to access the regime of this discrepancy
with particle-resolved techniques which might shed light on the origins of this discrepancy due to
the relatively sluggish dynamics of the larger colloids required for confocal microscopy.
Here we address this challenge with two developments. Our work is a marked improvement in
the precision of mapping the state point of experiments to simulation. For this, we employed a
combination of novel machine-learning methods for particle tracking and higher-order correlation
functions. Our second innovation is to consider the free energy of pre–critical nuclei which can be
detected in the discrepancy regime. These are in agreement with computer simulation. This is the
first time that such free energies have been directly compared between experiment and simulation
in any material as far as we are aware. The agreement provides important validation of rare event
sampling techniques which are used very widely in simulation, but which can seldom be directly
compared with experiment.
I.
INTRODUCTION
Crystal nucleation is a truly everyday phenomenon
with very wide–ranging industrial and environmental implications from purification of chemicals to crystallisation
of aerosol droplets being a major uncertainty in climate
change modelling [1]. It is clearly important to be able
to make meaningful predictions of the rate of nucleation
of crystallites. Despite very recent advances in atomistic
materials in a limited range of nucleation rates [2], the
comparison of nucleation rates between prediction and
experiment is woeful, from well-studied materials, water
[1], and in the case of NaCl, there is even significant discrepancy between different implementations of the same
computational model [3].
In such general challenges, model experimental systems, such as colloids, play an important role, as their
classical interactions make accurate large-scale computer
simulations possible, while their kinetics are convenient
from an experimental perspective [4, 5]. The kinetics are
controlled by the Brownian time taken by an isolated
sphere to diffuse by its own radius τB = 3πησ3/8kBT)
where η is the solvent viscosity.
However, in the most studied system, colloidal hard
spheres, as Fig. 1(b) shows, the discrepancy between experiment and simulation is as bad as in any system [5–8].
This discrepancy is important beyond the immediate application of nucleation because the rare event sampling
computational methods required here are used across the
molecular sciences from physics to biochemistry [9–11].
Direct comparison of rare event sampling is seldom possible with the level of detail available here, which renders
solution of this wild discrepancy all the more urgent.
In colloidal hard spheres, the nucleation rate vanishes
at the freezing boundary and increases dramatically upon
raising the chemical potential (or volume fraction in the
case of hard sphere colloids).
Here, two regimes can
be identified as shown in Fig. 1. At high supersaturation, where nucleation is rapid, experiment and simulation agree reasonably well. At low supersaturation where
nucleation is very slow, a huge discrepancy emerges as
shown by the shading in Fig. 1. The experiments in this
discrepancy regime were carried out using light scattering
in which the number and size of the nuclei is inferred indirectly [5, 7]. More recent work using confocal microscopy
where the coordinates of the particles can be tracked, offers the chance to measure more precisely the nuclei that
form [12] and to compare directly with predictions from
simulation. Alas, such data comes at a high price: colloids that are large enough to track (typically 2-3 µm in
diameter) have a Brownian time τB ∼10s, rendering rare
events like nucleation in weakly supersaturated suspensions inaccessible on reasonable experimental timescales.
There are then two possible reasons for the discrepancy:
either the nucleation rate is different between the experiments and that predicted by computer simulation, or
the state point is not mapped correctly between the two.
Until recently [13], accurate determination of the state
point, ie the volume fraction ϕ of an experimental colloidal system has been very difficult [14, 15].
Here we address the nucleation discrepancy with two
developments using real-space studies of colloids using
confocal microscopy. Firstly, we consider the nucleation
barrier. In classical nucleation theory (CNT), the nucleation rate

III.
RESULTS
We compare the experimental and simulated state
points using the radial distribution function g(r) in
Fig. 2(a). The agreement is very good indicating that
the state point is well matched. This is replicated in the
total correlation function shown in Appendix A.
However, we should note that g(r) is not a strong function of state point in this regime. Therefore, it is desirable to have a more precise probe of state point and here
we turn to higher-order correlations.
It is possible to
determine populations of clusters which minimise the local free energy of hard spheres [39] and the population
of these we show in Fig. 2(b). Overall, the agreement
between experiment and hard-sphere simulation is very
good, providing further evidence that the state point has
been well matched. The hard-core Yukawa simulations
have a a noticeably lower population of the larger cluster
sizes (m ≥10).

Properties of precritical nuclei. —
Our study naturally provides a large set of crystal nuclei particle coordinates, along with those of the surrounding fluid. We
now proceed to analyze the properties of these nuclei.
In Fig. 4(a) we show the asphericity of the nuclei. The
calculation is based on a simple Principle Component
Analysis and is discussed in the Materials and Methods
section. In terms of the asphericity, experiment and simulation are very well matched. Larger nuclei tend to be
more spherical, as shown in 4(b). The radius of gyration
Rg of the nuclei scales with the (n−1)th power, where
n is the number of constituent particles. The exponents
a and b obtained from experimental and simulation data
are nearly identical, and the fit of the scaling is excellent.
The asphericity and radius of gyration data show that the
pre-critical nuclei are well described by both experimental
and simulation data. The only exception is that in simulations, the asphericity is slightly higher for small clusters
(see the discussion in Section V).
V.
DISCUSSION
In this paper, we address the challenge of understanding the nucleation discrepancy between experiment and computer simulation in the context of hard sphere colloids. While the two have been widely used as model systems for nucleation, the state points are not always mapped accurately between the two. We present two key innovations: (1) precise mapping of the state point using higher-order correlations in the particle distribution, and (2) the determination of the free energy of formation of pre-critical nuclei. The agreement between experiment and simulation is the first time that such free energies have been directly compared in any material, and this level of validation provides significant confidence in the accuracy of rare event sampling techniques used in simulation.

The key findings are that the nucleation rate vanishes at the freezing boundary and increases dramatically upon crossing into the supersaturated regime. At low supersaturation, the simulations show that the nucleation barrier is lower than what is observed experimentally. This is the regime where the discrepancy is most pronounced. The two main reasons for the discrepancy are identified as (i) the mapping between the experiment and simulation state points and (ii) the free energy of the pre-critical nuclei. We have addressed both of these issues in the present work. The remaining discrepancy, if any, is due to factors that are not accounted for in the model. However, the agreement between experiment and simulation is so precise that it suggests that the model is capturing the essential physics of the problem.

The importance of this work lies in the fact that it provides a direct comparison between experiment and simulation in the same state point, which is essential for validating simulation models and improving our understanding of the nucleation process. Moreover, the determination of the free energy of the pre-critical nuclei opens up new possibilities for studying the thermodynamics of nucleation and for developing more accurate theoretical models.
V.1.
Limitations and Future Work
One limitation of our work is the relatively low number of particles in the simulation (N = 105), which limits our ability to sample rare events such as the formation of large nuclei. However, our focus is on the free energy of the pre-critical nuclei, which is accessible even with a small number of particles. Additionally, the experiments are performed in a hard-sphere system, which may not perfectly capture the behavior of real colloids with some degree of softness. Future work could involve extending the simulations to larger N, and exploring the effect of finite particle number on the free energy calculations. Another potential source of error is the choice of the bond-orientational order parameter q6, which may not capture all aspects of the nuclei's shape and structure. Future work could explore alternative order parameters or combine data from different order parameters to get a more complete picture of the nuclei's properties. Furthermore, the mapping between the experiment and simulation state points is still a challenge, and future work could aim to improve the precision of this mapping by incorporating additional observables or using more sophisticated analysis techniques. The free energy of the pre-critical nuclei is a key quantity in nucleation theory, and its accurate determination is crucial for validating and improving simulation models. Our work provides a significant step forward in this direction.

VI.
CONCLUSION
In conclusion, we have addressed the nucleation discrepancy in hard sphere colloids by combining precise particle tracking in experiments with advanced free energy calculations from computer simulations. We have shown that the nucleation barrier can be directly measured and compared between experiment and simulation, and that the two systems agree remarkably well when the state points are accurately mapped. This study provides a benchmark for future work in nucleation theory, and opens up new avenues for understanding the thermodynamics of nucleation in colloidal systems.
